The radar cross section (RCS) is a measure of the scattered power from a target towards the radar receiver.
PEMC media are characterized by a scalar admittance parameter M, with PEC and PMC as limiting cases (M → ±∞ and M = 0 respectively).
The study analyzes a PEMC strip embedded in four different soil models: dry soil and San Antonio clay loam with 5%, 10%, and 20% water content.
Increasing soil moisture content increases electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity, leading to higher attenuation of scattered fields.
The cross-polarized scattered field component is zero for PEC and PMC cases and maximal for PEMC with M = ±1.
The scattered field from the PEMC strip exhibits nonreciprocal behavior due to the cross-polarized component.
The RCS amplitude and scattering width decrease as the soil conductivity and permittivity increase.
Numerical results were generated using Mathematica software reproducing Lindell and Sihvola's PEMC theory.
The interference nulls in the RCS pattern disappear in lossy soil media due to attenuation of diffracted energy from the strip edges.
The radar cross section depends on frequency, polarization, aspect angle, soil properties, and strip dimensions.
Physical optics and geometrical optics approximations are used to calculate the scattered fields from the finite-width strip.
The soil dielectric constant model includes complex relative permittivity with real and imaginary parts dependent on frequency and moisture.
The study focuses on a frequency of 1 GHz for numerical evaluation of scattering widths.
The duality transformation relates the scattered fields of PEC strips to those of PEMC strips.
The scattered field expressions involve induced surface currents approximated by physical optics currents.
The RCS is computed as a function of observation angle and strip geometry in a lossy half-space.
The paper provides analytical formulas for the scattered fields and scattering width of PEMC strips.
The cross-polarized scattered field leads to a nonreciprocal scattering effect unique to PEMC materials.
The study contributes to understanding electromagnetic wave scattering for ground penetrating radar applications.
The strip is modeled as a two-dimensional finite-width strip embedded in a lossy medium.
